name: Describing the solution space from a reduced row echelon matrix
text:
Consider the reduced row echelon matrix $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp 2 \amp -1 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array} \right] $$ and its corresponding linear system as $$ \begin{alignedat}{4} x \amp \amp \amp {}+{} \amp 2z \amp {}={} \amp -1 \\ \amp \amp y \amp {}+{} \amp z \amp {}={} \amp 2. \\ \end{alignedat} $$ Let's rewrite the equations as $$ \begin{alignedat}{2} x \amp {}={} \amp -1 -2z\\ y \amp {}={} \amp 2-z. \\ \end{alignedat} $$ From this description, it is clear that we obtain a solution for any value of the variable $z$. For instance, if $z=2$, then $x = -5$ and $y=0$ so that $(x,y,z) = (-5,0,2)$ is a solution. Similarly, if $z=0$, we see that $(x,y,z) = (-1,2,0)$ is also a solution.

Because there is no restriction on the value of $z$, we call it a free variable, and note that the linear system has infinitely many solutions. The variables $x$ and $ y$ are called basic variables as they are determined once we make a choice of the free variable.

We will call this description of the solution space, in which the basic variables are written in terms of the free variables, a parametric description of the solution space.

Consider the matrix $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 4 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp -3 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \amp 1 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ \end{array} \right]. $$ The last equation gives $$ 0x +0y+0z = 0$$ , which is true for any $(x,y,z)$. We may safely ignore this equation since it does not impose a restriction on $(x,y,z)$. We then see that there is a unique solution $(x,y,z) = (4,-3,1)$.

Consider the matrix $$ \left[ \begin{array}{rrr|r} 1 \amp 0 \amp 2 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp -1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array} \right]. $$ Beginning with the last equation, we see that $$ 0x +0y+0z = 0 = 1$$ , which is not true for any $(x,y,z)$. There is no solution to this particular equation and therefore no solution to the system of equations.
